entries.1:1: Amos was a sheep farmer, not a professional prophet, yet God gave him a message about Israel during the reigns of two kings. This shows God can use ordinary people to speak his truth, and that he warns people before judgment comes.
entries.1:2: God is pictured as roaring like a lion from Jerusalem, a sound so powerful that even the pastures dry up. It means God is about to act in judgment, and no one can ignore his voice.
entries.1:3: God says Damascus has committed crime after crime, and he will not overlook it, because they brutally crushed the people of Gilead. This means God sees cruelty and will hold nations accountable for it.
entries.1:4: God will send fire on the royal house of Damascus, destroying the palaces of its kings. It means the powerful leaders who did evil will not escape judgment.
entries.1:5: God will break Damascus's defenses, remove its rulers, and send its people into exile. It means no nation's strength or security can protect it from God's judgment.
entries.1:6: God says Gaza has committed crime after crime, because they captured whole communities and sold them as slaves to Edom. This means God cares about human trafficking and will judge those who treat people as goods.
entries.1:7: God will send fire on Gaza's walls and burn its palaces. It means the city's defenses and wealth will not save it from judgment.
entries.1:8: God will cut off the rulers of Ashdod and Ashkelon and turn against Ekron, and the remaining Philistines will be destroyed. It means God will deal with each city that took part in the evil, and none will escape.
entries.1:9: God says Tyre has committed crime after crime, because they handed whole populations over to Edom as slaves, ignoring their treaty of brotherhood. This means breaking promises and betraying allies matters to God.
entries.1:10: God will send fire on Tyre's walls and burn its palaces. It means even a wealthy, well-defended city cannot stand against God's judgment.
entries.1:11: God says Edom has committed crime after crime, because they attacked their own brother with the sword and showed no pity, nursing anger endlessly. This means God takes family betrayal and unforgiving hatred seriously.
entries.1:12: God will send fire on Teman and burn the palaces of Bozrah. It means Edom's strongholds and leaders will be destroyed for their cruelty.
entries.1:13: God says Ammon has committed crime after crime, because they brutally killed pregnant women to expand their territory. This means God sees even the worst violence against the innocent and will judge it.
entries.1:14: God will set fire to the walls of Rabbah, and its palaces will burn amid the noise of battle and storm. It means war and destruction will come on Ammon because of its cruelty.
entries.1:15: Ammon's king and his officers will be taken away as prisoners. It means the leaders who ordered such evil will be humbled and carried off, just as they did to others.
entries.2:1: God says Moab will be punished for a cruel act: burning the bones of Edom's king to dust, which showed deep disrespect for the dead. It means God notices cruelty done to others, even when it happens between nations.
entries.2:2: Because of that cruelty, God warns that fire and war will come to Moab's cities, with the alarm of battle and people crying out. It means wrongdoing brings real consequences, and no nation escapes God's attention.
entries.2:3: God says he will remove Moab's ruler and put its leaders to death. It means those in charge are accountable to God for how their people act.
entries.2:4: God says Judah will be punished because the people rejected his law and followed the false ways of their ancestors. It means ignoring what God has taught us and copying bad examples leads us away from what is right.
entries.2:5: God warns that fire will come on Judah and burn the great buildings of Jerusalem. It means even God's own people face judgment when they turn away from him.
entries.2:6: God says Israel will be punished because they sell honest people for money and sell the poor for the price of a pair of shoes. It means treating people as things to be bought and sold is a serious wrong in God's eyes.
entries.2:7: The powerful crush the poor and push humble people off their path, and men commit sexual sin that dishonors God's name. It means God cares how the weak are treated and how his name is respected.
entries.2:8: People lie on clothes taken as pledges from debtors and drink wine taken as fines in the house of their god. It means using religion to cover up greed and injustice makes worship empty.
entries.2:9: God reminds Israel that he destroyed the powerful Amorites before them, a people described as tall and strong. It means God had already done great things for them, so their wrongdoing is especially serious.
entries.2:10: God reminds them that he brought them out of Egypt and led them through the desert for forty years to give them the land. It means they owe their whole existence and homeland to God's kindness.
entries.2:11: God says he raised up prophets and set apart young men for himself from among their own people. It means God gave them spiritual gifts and leaders as a sign of his care.
entries.2:12: But the people made those set apart drink wine and told the prophets to stop prophesying. It means they rejected God's gifts and silenced his messengers.
entries.2:13: God says he will crush them down like a cart loaded with grain presses down on what is under it. It means their resistance cannot hold up under the weight of God's judgment.
entries.2:14: When that happens, fast runners will find no escape and strong men will lose their strength, and soldiers will not get away safely. It means human speed and power cannot save anyone from God's judgment.
entries.2:15: Archers will not hold their ground, fast runners will not escape, and horsemen will not save their lives. It means every kind of military skill will fail in that day.
entries.2:16: Even the bravest soldier will run away naked in that day, says the Lord. It means the most fearless will be stripped of courage and dignity when God acts.
entries.3:1: God is speaking directly to the people of Israel, the nation he rescued from slavery in Egypt, and telling them to listen carefully to his message against them. It means God's words are meant for them personally, and they should pay attention because he is the one who brought them out.
entries.3:2: God says that out of all the nations on earth, he chose and cared for Israel in a special way, so their sins deserve a special response from him. It means being close to God brings greater responsibility, and the reader should take their own wrongdoing seriously.
entries.3:3: Two people cannot walk together in the same direction unless they have agreed on where they are going. It means agreement is needed for a shared path, and the reader should think about whether they are truly in step with God.
entries.3:4: A lion does not roar in the woods unless it has caught something, and a young lion does not growl from its den without a reason. It means every action has a cause, and the reader should understand that God's warnings are not empty noise.
entries.3:5: A bird is not caught in a trap on the ground unless a trap has been set, and a net does not spring up unless something has triggered it. It means events do not happen without a reason, and the reader should recognize that consequences follow causes.
entries.3:6: When a warning horn sounds in a town, people are afraid, and when disaster comes to a city, it is the Lord who has allowed it. It means God is involved in what happens in the world, and the reader should take his warnings seriously rather than ignore them.
entries.3:7: The Lord does not do anything without first revealing his plan to the prophets who serve him. It means God warns people before he acts, and the reader can trust that he does not act without giving notice.
entries.3:8: When a lion roars, people are afraid, and when the Lord God speaks, his prophet cannot stay silent. It means God's word is powerful and demands a response, and the reader should listen when God speaks rather than dismiss it.
entries.3:9: God tells the great powers of Assyria and Egypt to gather and look at the violence and cruelty happening in Samaria, Israel's capital. It means Israel's wrongdoing is being exposed publicly, and the reader should realize that injustice does not stay hidden.
entries.3:10: The Lord says the people do not know how to do what is right, and they fill their grand houses with things taken by violence and destruction. It means their wealth came from wrongdoing, and the reader should examine whether their own gain is honest.
entries.3:11: The Lord declares that an enemy will surround the land, break down its strength, and plunder its great houses. It means judgment is coming because of their sin, and the reader should see that security built on wrongdoing does not last.
entries.3:12: Just as a shepherd rescues only a couple of legs or a piece of an ear from a lion's mouth, so only a small remnant of Israel will escape. It means the rescue will be minimal, and the reader should understand that sin brings serious loss.
entries.3:13: God, the Lord of all heavenly armies, calls for witnesses to testify against the family of Jacob, meaning the people of Israel. It means their wrongdoing is being formally charged, and the reader should take God's case against sin seriously.
entries.3:14: When God punishes Israel for their sins, he will also destroy the altars at Bethel, cutting off their horns and throwing them to the ground. It means their places of false worship will be torn down, and the reader should not rely on religious symbols while ignoring God.
entries.3:15: God will destroy both the winter and summer houses, the ivory-decorated houses, and the great mansions, so they all come to an end. It means their luxurious homes will not save them, and the reader should not put their trust in wealth or possessions.
entries.4:1: The prophet calls the rich women of Samaria fat cows because they live in luxury while crushing the poor and demanding more wine from their husbands. It warns that comfortable people who ignore the needy are not safe from God's judgment.
entries.4:2: God swears by his own holy name that these wealthy people will be dragged away like fish on hooks into exile. It means their privilege will not protect them; God keeps his word.
entries.4:3: The women will be led out through gaps in the broken city walls and taken away to a foreign place. It means the fall of their city will be humiliating and inescapable.
entries.4:4: God tells the people to keep going to their shrines at Bethel and Gilgal and pile up more sin with their frequent offerings. It means religious activity without real obedience only adds to guilt.
entries.4:5: They proudly burn leavened bread as a praise offering and announce their freewill gifts publicly because they enjoy the attention. It means showing off religion for people's approval is not what God wants.
entries.4:6: God had already sent hunger and empty pantries in every town, yet the people still did not turn back to him. It means hardship is meant to wake us up, and ignoring it leaves us unchanged.
entries.4:7: God held back rain three months before harvest and sent it on one town but not another, so fields dried up. It means even the weather is under God's control and can be a call to return to him.
entries.4:8: People staggered from town to town looking for water and never had enough, yet they still did not return to God. It means scarcity should drive us to God, not just to desperate searching.
entries.4:9: God struck their crops with blight and mildew, and worms ate their gardens, vines, fig trees and olive trees, yet they did not return. It means repeated losses are warnings we should not ignore.
entries.4:10: God sent plagues like Egypt's, killed young men in war, took their horses, and left the stench of death in their camps, yet they did not return. It means even severe suffering did not move them to repent.
entries.4:11: God overthrew some of them as he did Sodom and Gomorrah, leaving them like a stick snatched from a fire, yet they did not return. It means they were rescued from total ruin but still refused to change.
entries.4:12: Because God will act against Israel, he tells them to prepare to meet their God. It means judgment is certain, so people should get ready to face the God they have ignored.
entries.4:13: This verse describes God as the one who formed the mountains, made the wind, reveals his plans to people, and rules over all the earth. It means the God who judges is the all-powerful Creator, so his warning deserves serious attention.
entries.5:1: God is speaking through the prophet as if singing a funeral song over Israel before the disaster even happens. It means the reader should take God's warning seriously, because he grieves over the harm his people bring on themselves.
entries.5:2: Israel is pictured as a young woman who has fallen and cannot get up, with no one to help her. The point is that the nation's collapse will be total and no one will be able to rescue it.
entries.5:3: A town that once sent out a thousand soldiers will send only a hundred, and one that sent a hundred will send only ten. It means the nation's strength will be cut down drastically because of its sin.
entries.5:4: God tells his people the one thing that can save them: turn back to him wholeheartedly. It means real life is found in coming back to God, not in anything else.
entries.5:5: God warns them not to run to famous shrines like Bethel, Gilgal, or Beersheba for safety, because those places will be destroyed. It means trusting in religious places or rituals instead of God is useless.
entries.5:6: They should seek the Lord himself so they can live, or his judgment will break out like an unstoppable fire. It means the reader should turn to God now, before it is too late.
entries.5:7: These people turn justice into something bitter and push what is right down to the ground. It means God sees when people twist fairness and trample on what is good.
entries.5:8: God is the one who made the stars, turns darkness into morning and day into night, and controls the seas. It means the God who calls you to justice is the all-powerful Creator, not a small local deity.
entries.5:9: He brings sudden ruin on the strong and breaks down fortified towns. It means no human power or wall can stand against God's judgment.
entries.5:10: They hate anyone who speaks up against wrongdoing in public and can't stand honest people. It means a society is in trouble when it resents those who tell the truth.
entries.5:11: Because they crush the poor and tax them on their grain, they will build fine stone houses but never live in them, and plant vineyards but never drink the wine. It means wealth taken from the poor brings no real enjoyment.
entries.5:12: God knows their many sins: they harass honest people, take bribes, and deny justice to the poor in court. It means God sees corruption and injustice even when it looks normal to everyone else.
entries.5:13: In such evil times, wise people will keep quiet because speaking up does no good. It means there are times when evil is so entrenched that even wise words are useless.
entries.5:14: Seek good and not evil so you may live, and then God will truly be with you as you claim. It means God's presence is shown by a life that actually pursues what is good.
entries.5:15: Hate evil, love good, and make sure justice is done in public, and perhaps God will spare the survivors. It means real change means loving good and working for fair treatment of others, not just saying the right words.
entries.5:16: God says there will be weeping everywhere, in every square and street, and even farmers and singers will be called to mourn. It means the coming judgment will bring widespread grief that no one can avoid.
entries.5:17: There will be cries of grief in every vineyard because God himself will pass through their midst. It means the disaster is not random bad luck but God's own response to their sin.
entries.5:18: People longing for the day of the Lord should beware, because for them it will be darkness, not light. It means expecting God to show up on your side while you keep sinning is a dangerous mistake.
entries.5:19: It's like escaping a lion only to meet a bear, or reaching your house and getting bitten by a snake. It means there will be no safe place to hide from the coming judgment.
entries.5:20: Yes, the day of the Lord will be dark, very dark, with no light at all. It means God's judgment on unrepentant people is serious and inescapable.
entries.5:21: God says their festivals disgust him and he wants nothing to do with their religious gatherings. It means God is not impressed by religious activity when the heart and life are wrong.
entries.5:22: Even their burnt offerings, grain offerings, and peace offerings bring God no pleasure. It means going through religious motions cannot buy off God or cover up injustice.
entries.5:23: God tells them to stop the noise of their songs and shuts his ears to their music. It means worship that comes from people who ignore justice is just noise to God.
entries.5:24: Instead, let justice roll on like a river and righteousness like a stream that never runs dry. It means God wants fair and right living to flow constantly from his people, more than he wants songs.
entries.5:25: God asks whether Israel really brought him offerings during the forty years in the wilderness. It means their religious ceremonies were never the point; God has always cared about the heart.
entries.5:26: They carried the idols of their own making, Sikkuth and Kiyyun, instead of trusting God. It means people easily replace God with things they have made themselves.
entries.5:27: So God will send them into exile far beyond Damascus, says the Lord, the God of armies. It means rejecting God leads to real consequences, and the powerful God who says this will carry it out.
entries.6:1: God warns the wealthy and important people who feel safe and comfortable that their security is false. Being at ease while ignoring danger invites judgment, so readers should not confuse comfort with safety.
entries.6:2: God tells them to look at other great cities that were already ruined and ask whether they are any better or stronger. Their pride is misplaced, because no nation is immune to downfall.
entries.6:3: They push thoughts of coming disaster far away and instead welcome violence and injustice. Refusing to face the truth about wrongdoing only makes the coming judgment worse.
entries.6:4: They live in luxury, lounging on fancy furniture and eating the best meat every day. Their self-indulgence shows how far their hearts are from God and from the suffering around them.
entries.6:5: They entertain themselves with music and invent instruments, imitating David's worship but without his heart for God. Enjoyment of art and music becomes empty when it replaces devotion and care for others.
entries.6:6: They drink extravagantly and use expensive oils on themselves, yet feel no sorrow over the ruin of their own people. God condemns living in pleasure while being indifferent to others' suffering.
entries.6:7: Because of this, the first to be taken into exile will be these comfortable leaders, and their parties will end. Those who live only for pleasure will lose it suddenly.
entries.6:8: God swears by himself that he despises the pride of Israel and their grand houses, and he will hand over the city and all it contains. Pride and self-reliance provoke God's judgment.
entries.6:9: Even if ten people remain hiding in one house, death will still find them. No amount of hiding or numbers can escape the judgment God has announced.
entries.6:10: A relative comes to remove the dead bodies, and when he learns no one is left alive, he tells people to be silent and not invoke the Lord's name. The horror is so great that even speaking God's name seems dangerous.
entries.6:11: At the Lord's command, both the great house and the small house will be smashed and shattered. Judgment will reach every level of society, rich and poor alike.
entries.6:12: Just as horses cannot run on solid rock and oxen cannot plow the sea, justice cannot be twisted into poison without disaster. When people turn right into wrong, the result is ruin.
entries.6:13: They boast over a worthless victory and claim they won by their own strength. Taking credit for power that is not really theirs leads to false confidence and downfall.
entries.6:14: God declares that he will bring a foreign nation to crush Israel from one end of the land to the other. The very power they trusted in will be used against them.
entries.7:1: God showed Amos a vision of locusts coming to eat the crops just as the late grass was sprouting after the king's share had been cut. It means God was warning his people that disaster was about to strip away their food supply.
entries.7:2: When the locusts had eaten everything, Amos begged God to forgive and spare his people, because they were small and couldn't survive such a blow. It shows that praying for mercy when trouble comes is the right response.
entries.7:3: God relented and said this judgment would not happen. It means God listens when someone pleads for mercy and can hold back disaster.
entries.7:4: God showed Amos another vision, of a great fire that would burn up the deep waters and threaten to destroy the land God had given his people. It means God was warning that a sweeping judgment was coming.
entries.7:5: Amos again begged God to stop, asking how his small people could possibly survive. It shows that faithful prayer keeps asking God to spare those who are weak.
entries.7:6: God again changed his mind and said this too would not happen. It means God's mercy can turn aside the disaster he had threatened.
entries.7:7: God showed Amos a vision of himself standing beside a wall built straight with a weighted line, holding that line in his hand. It means God was about to measure his people against his standard to see if they were straight.
entries.7:8: God asked Amos what he saw, and when Amos said a weighted line, God said he would hold his people to that standard and would no longer overlook their sin. It means God's patience had run out and he would now judge them honestly.
entries.7:9: God said the places where Isaac and Israel worshiped would be destroyed and the family of King Jeroboam would be killed by the sword. It means judgment would fall on both their false worship and their royal house.
entries.7:10: Amaziah, the priest at Bethel, sent word to King Jeroboam that Amos was plotting against him and stirring up the country with his words. It shows that people often attack the messenger when they don't want to hear the message.
entries.7:11: Amaziah reported that Amos had predicted the king would die by the sword and the people would be dragged away as prisoners. It means the priest twisted the prophet's warning into a charge of treason.
entries.7:12: Amaziah told Amos to run away to Judah and earn his living as a prophet there. It means he wanted Amos silenced and pushed out of the country.
entries.7:13: Amaziah told him to stop prophesying at Bethel, calling it the king's holy place and the king's house. It means the priest was protecting the king's interests instead of listening to God.
entries.7:14: Amos answered that he was not a professional prophet or from a prophet's family; he was a herdsman who also tended sycamore trees. It means God can call ordinary working people to speak his word.
entries.7:15: Amos said the Lord had taken him away from his flock and told him to go and prophesy to Israel. It means his message came from God's direct call, not from his own ambition.
entries.7:16: Amos told Amaziah to listen to the Lord's word, since Amaziah had ordered him to stop prophesying against Israel. It means no one can silence what God has commanded his messenger to say.
entries.7:17: God declared through Amos that Amaziah's wife would be shamed in the city, his children killed, his land divided up, and he himself would die in a foreign land, while Israel would be taken away as prisoners. It means opposing God's word brings serious consequences on the one who does it and on the nation.
entries.8:1: God shows Amos a basket of ripe summer fruit. It looks ordinary, but it is a picture that something is now fully ripe and ready to be dealt with.
entries.8:2: God asks Amos what he sees, then explains the meaning: Israel's time is up, and God will no longer overlook their sin. The reader should take seriously that God's patience does have an end.
entries.8:3: In that day the happy songs in the royal palace will turn into wails of grief, and so many will die that bodies are dumped everywhere in silence. It shows how complete the coming judgment will be.
entries.8:4: God speaks to those who trample on the poor and are determined to wipe out the needy in the land. The reader is warned that mistreating the vulnerable puts you under God's judgment.
entries.8:5: These people can't wait for religious holidays to end so they can get back to selling grain, and they cheat by using small measures, high prices, and rigged scales. It shows that greed can turn even worship into an inconvenience.
entries.8:6: They buy the poor for silver and the needy for the price of a pair of sandals, and they even sell the worthless scraps of grain. The reader sees how far people will go when money matters more than people.
entries.8:7: The Lord swears by the pride of Jacob that he will never forget any of their deeds. It means God remembers wrongdoing and will not let it slide forever.
entries.8:8: Because of this the land will tremble and everyone in it will mourn, and it will rise and fall like the flooding Nile. The reader should see that sin brings upheaval and sorrow to whole communities.
entries.8:9: God says that on that day he will make the sun go down at noon and darken the earth in broad daylight. It is a picture of sudden, unnatural disaster in the middle of ordinary life.
entries.8:10: Their festivals will become funerals, their music will turn to mourning, and people will shave their heads and wear rough cloth as they grieve, like parents mourning an only son. The reader sees that joy can be turned to bitter sorrow overnight.
entries.8:11: God says a time is coming when the land will hunger, not for food or water, but for hearing his words. The worst famine is being cut off from God's voice.
entries.8:12: People will wander from sea to sea and from north to east, searching everywhere for a word from the Lord, but they won't find it. The reader is warned not to take God's word for granted while it is available.
entries.8:13: On that day even the strong and beautiful young people will faint from thirst. It shows that no one's youth or strength will protect them from the coming hardship.
entries.8:14: Those who swear by the false gods of Samaria, Dan, and Beersheba will fall and never get up again. The reader learns that trusting in anything other than the living God leads to ruin.
entries.9:1: God is shown standing at the altar, striking the pillars so the building shakes, and announcing that no one will escape the coming judgment. For the reader, it means God himself is the one bringing judgment, and there is no hiding place from him.
entries.9:2: Even if people dig down into the world of the dead or climb up to heaven, God says his hand will reach them. It means no location, however extreme, puts anyone beyond God's reach.
entries.9:3: If they hide on top of Mount Carmel or at the bottom of the sea, God will search them out and command even the sea creature to strike them. It means hiding cannot save a person from God's judgment.
entries.9:4: Even if enemies capture them and carry them away, God will command the sword to kill them there. It means God's attention is set on them for punishment, not for good, so no escape route works.
entries.9:5: The Lord of heavenly armies is so powerful that his touch melts the land and makes everyone mourn, rising and falling like the Nile. It means the God who judges is the almighty ruler over all the earth.
entries.9:6: God builds his upper rooms in the sky and sets the foundation of his dwelling on the earth, and he commands the sea waters to flood the land. It means the same God who controls the whole cosmos is the one speaking, so his word cannot be dismissed.
entries.9:7: God asks Israel whether they are really any different to him from the Ethiopians, since he also brought the Philistines and Arameans out of other lands. It means Israel should not assume God's favor means they are exempt from his standards.
entries.9:8: God's eyes are on the sinful kingdom to destroy it from the earth, yet he promises not to wipe out the family of Jacob completely. It means judgment is real, but God still keeps a remnant and does not abandon his people entirely.
entries.9:9: God will shake Israel among the nations the way grain is shaken in a sieve, yet not one true grain will fall to the ground and be lost. It means the scattering is for sifting, and God carefully preserves those who belong to him.
entries.9:10: Those among God's people who say disaster will never touch them will die by the sword. It means complacent confidence that judgment will not come is itself a deadly mistake.
entries.9:11: God promises to raise up David's fallen tent, repair its broken places, and rebuild it as it was long ago. It means God will restore the ruined dynasty of David and bring back what was lost.
entries.9:12: The restored people will possess what is left of Edom and all the nations that bear God's name. It means God's restoration will extend beyond Israel to include other peoples.
entries.9:13: Days are coming when the harvest will be so abundant that ploughing and reaping overlap, and wine will flow down the mountains and hills. It means God's future blessing will be overflowing and unstoppable.
entries.9:14: God will restore his people Israel so they rebuild ruined towns, plant vineyards and drink the wine, and make gardens and eat the fruit. It means the restored life will be settled, productive, and enjoyed, not just survived.
entries.9:15: God will plant his people firmly in their own land and never uproot them again. It means their place with him will be permanent and secure, guaranteed by God himself.
